x.ASV: Awake, awake, put on thy strength, O Zion; put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into thee the uncircumcised and the unclean.

x.KJV: Awake, awake; put on thy strength, O Zion; put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into thee the uncircumcised and the unclean.
x.YLT: Awake, awake, put on thy strength, O Zion, Put on the garments of thy beauty, Jerusalem--the Holy City; For enter no more into thee again, Do the uncircumcised and unclean.

nt: Isaiah is repeating forms of the verb **Awake** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Wake up completely]

Isaiah is speaking of strength as if it were clothing that Zion could put on. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [make yourself strong]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [city that is set apart for God]

Isaiah is using the adjectives **uncircumcised** and **unclean** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [uncircumcised people or unclean people]

x.ASV: Shake thyself from the dust; arise, sit on thy throne, O Jerusalem: loose thyself from the bonds of thy neck, O captive daughter of Zion.
x.Darby: Shake thyself from the dust; arise, sit down, Jerusalem: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck, captive daughter of Zion.
x.KJV: Shake thyself from the dust; arise, and sit down, O Jerusalem: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck, O captive daughter of Zion.
x.YLT: Shake thyself from dust, arise, sit, O Jerusalem, Bands of thy neck have loosed themselves, O captive, daughter of Zion.

nt: Isaiah is speaking of mourning as if it were **dust** that Jerusalem could **shake** off. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Stop mourning]

Isaiah is speaking of Jerusalem’s captivity as if it were **bonds** around her **neck**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the captivity that binds you]

Isaiah is speaking of the city of Zion as if it were a woman who had been taken **captive**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you people of Zion who have been taken captive]

x.ASV: For thus saith Jehovah, Ye were sold for nought; and ye shall be redeemed without money.
x.Darby: For thus saith Jehovah: Ye have sold yourselves for nought, and ye shall be redeemed without money.
x.KJV: For thus saith the Lord, Ye have sold yourselves for nought; and ye shall be redeemed without money.
x.YLT: For thus said Jehovah: `For nought ye have been sold, And not by money are ye redeemed.'

nt: Yahweh is speaking of his people going into captivity as if they had been sold, and of their release as if they would be redeemed with a payment. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You were taken captive for no payment, and it will not be with silver that you are set free]

The expression **You were sold** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I sold you for nothing]

The expression **will you be redeemed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will I redeem you]

x.ASV: For thus saith the Lord Jehovah, My people went down at the first into Egypt to sojourn there: and the Assyrian hath oppressed them without cause.
x.Darby: For thus saith the Lord Jehovah: My people went down at the first into Egypt to sojourn there, and Assyria oppressed them without cause;
x.KJV: For thus saith the Lord God, My people went down aforetime into Egypt to sojourn there; and the Assyrian oppressed them without cause.
x.YLT: For thus said the Lord Jehovah: `To Egypt My people went down at first to sojourn there, And Asshur--for nought he hath oppressed it.

nt: In this verse, the word **him** is singular in form, but it refers to all of Yahweh’s people as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “him.” Alternate translation: [and Assyria oppressed them]

x.ASV: Now therefore, what do I here, saith Jehovah, seeing that my people is taken away for nought? they that rule over them do howl, saith Jehovah, and my name continually all the day is blasphemed.
x.Darby: and now, what have I here, saith Jehovah, that my people hath been taken away for nought? They that rule over them make them to howl, saith Jehovah; and continually all the day is my name scorned.
x.KJV: Now therefore, what have I here, saith the Lord, that my people is taken away for nought? they that rule over them make them to howl, saith the Lord; and my name continually every day is blasphemed.
x.YLT: And now, what--to Me here, An affirmation of Jehovah, That taken is My people for nought? Its rulers cause howling, --an affirmation of Jehovah, And continually all the day My name is despised.

nt: Yahweh is using the question form to express his indignation over what is happening to his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [there is nothing left for me here!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **declaration**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [this is what Yahweh declares]

The expression **my people is taken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [enemies have taken my people]

The expression **my name is being despised** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people are despising my name]
Here, **my name** represents “my reputation.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my honor]

x.ASV: Therefore my people shall know my name: therefore they shall know in that day that I am he that doth speak; behold, it is I.
x.Darby: Therefore my people shall know my name; therefore [they shall know] in that day that I [am] HE, that saith, Here am I.
x.KJV: Therefore my people shall know my name: therefore they shall know in that day that I am he that doth speak: behold, it is I.
x.YLT: Therefore doth My people know My name, Therefore, in that day, Surely I am He who is speaking, behold Me.'

nt: Here, **my name** represents “who I truly am.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my people will know who I truly am]

x.ASV: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace, that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation, that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
x.Darby: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that announceth glad tidings, that publisheth peace; that announceth glad tidings of good, that publisheth salvation, that saith unto Zion, ThyGod reigneth!
x.KJV: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
x.YLT: How comely on the mountains, Have been the feet of one proclaiming tidings, Sounding peace, proclaiming good tidings, Sounding salvation, Saying to Zion, `Reigned hath thy God.'

nt: Isaiah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of admiration. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How very beautiful they are on the mountains]

Here, **the feet of the one heralding** represents the arrival of the messenger who brings news. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the ones heralding, as they arrive]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one making one hear that God will save people]

The messenger is not using this possessive form **Your God** to indicate that the people of Zion possess or control Yahweh. Rather, the messenger is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the people of Zion worship. Alternate translation: [The God you worship]

x.ASV: The voice of thy watchmen! they lift up the voice, together do they sing; for they shall see eye to eye, when Jehovah returneth to Zion.
x.Darby: — The voice of thy watchmen, they lift up the voice, they sing aloud together; for they shall see eye to eye, when Jehovah shall bring again Zion.
x.KJV: Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice; with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye, when the Lord shall bring again Zion.
x.YLT: The voice of thy watchmen! They have lifted up the voice, together they cry aloud, Because eye to eye they see, in Jehovah's turning back to Zion.

nt: עַ֤יִן בְּ⁠עַ֨יִן֙ יִרְא֔וּ בְּ⁠שׁ֥וּב יְהוָ֖ה צִיּֽוֹן

Isaiah is using **eye to eye** as a common expression of the culture to mean “clearly” or “unobstructedly.” The idea is that the Judeans will see Yahweh returning and there will be nothing between their eyes and his eyes. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. (In some languages, seeing eye to eye means being in agreement. That is not the meaning here, although the context indicates that there will be complete harmony between Yahweh and his people.) Alternate translation: [they will directly see Yahweh is returning to Zion]

This could mean: (1) that Yahweh will be helping Zion again. The UST models one way to express that meaning. (2) Yahweh will be **returning** the exiles from Judah. Alternate translation: [at the people whom Yahweh is returning to Zion]

x.ASV: Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem; for Jehovah hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem.
x.Darby: Break forth, sing aloud together, waste places of Jerusalem; for Jehovah comforteth his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem.
x.KJV: Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem: for the Lord hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem.
x.YLT: Break forth, sing together, O wastes of Jerusalem, For Jehovah hath comforted His people, He hath redeemed Jerusalem.

nt: Isaiah is speaking of the **desolations of Jerusalem** as if they were living things that could **sing joyfully**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [desolated Jerusalem, welcome your people]

x.ASV: Jehovah hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.
x.Darby: Jehovah hath made bare his holy arm in the sight of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of ourGod.

x.YLT: Jehovah hath made bare His holy arm Before the eyes of all the nations, And seen have all the ends of the earth, The salvation of our God.

nt: Here, **the arm** represents Yahweh’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his holy strength]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his holy arm]

Here, **all of the ends of the earth** represents all the people who live in the most distant places on earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [people everywhere in the world]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how our God saves us]

x.ASV: Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence, touch no unclean thing; go ye out of the midst of her; cleanse yourselves, ye that bear the vessels of Jehovah.
x.Darby: — Depart, depart, go out from thence, touch not what is unclean; go out of the midst of her, be ye clean, that bear the vessels of Jehovah.
x.KJV: Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence, touch no unclean thing; go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the Lord.
x.YLT: Turn aside, turn aside, go out thence, The unclean touch not, go out from her midst, Be ye pure, who are bearing the weapons of Jehovah.

nt: Isaiah is repeating forms of the phrase **Turn aside** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Turn aside quickly]

Isaiah is using the adjective **unclean** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [May you not touch anything that is unclean]

x.ASV: For ye shall not go out in haste, neither shall ye go by flight: for Jehovah will go before you; and the God of Israel will be your rearward.
x.Darby: For ye shall not go out with haste, nor go by flight; for Jehovah will go before you, and theGod of Israel will be your rear-guard.
x.KJV: For ye shall not go out with haste, nor go by flight: for the Lord will go before you; and the God of Israel will be your rereward.
x.YLT: For not in haste do ye go out, Yea, with flight ye go not on, For going before you is Jehovah, And gathering you is the God of Israel!

nt: Here, **going to your faces** represents going ahead of you. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [will be going ahead of you]

The expression **assembling you** is complementary to **going to your faces**. The idea is that Yahweh will be both leading the Israelites and going behind them to protect them. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the God of Israel will be your rear guard] or [and the God of Israel will be herding in the stragglers]

t: and/ he will be lifted up

x.ASV: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
x.Darby: Behold, my servant shall deal prudently; he shall be exalted and be lifted up, and be very high.
x.KJV: Behold, my servant shall deal prudently, he shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high.
x.YLT: Lo, My servant doth act wisely, He is high, and hath been lifted up, And hath been very high.

nt: Yahweh is speaking of his servant being greatly honored as if the servant would physically become **high**, be **lifted up**, and be **very lofty**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will be greatly honored, and he will be exalted, and he will be highly esteemed]
This could mean: (1) will succeed. Alternate translation: [be successful] or (2) will act wisely. Alternate translation: [will act wisely]

The expression **he will be lifted up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God will lift him up]

x.ASV: Like as many were astonished at thee (his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men),
x.Darby: As many were astonished at thee — his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the children of men
x.KJV: As many were astonied at thee; his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men:
x.YLT: As astonished at thee have been many, (So marred by man his appearance, And his form by sons of men.)

nt: Even though Yahweh is addressing Isaiah directly as **you**, he then speaks of him in the third person, referring to **his form**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this consistently in the second person. Alternate translation: [will marvel at you … your appearance, and your form]

Some ancient manuscripts read “at you.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “at him.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **disfigurement**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his appearance will be disfigured]

Yahweh is using **the sons of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [more than that of other humans]

x.ASV: so shall he sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths at him: for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they understand.
x.Darby: — so shall he astonish many nations; kings shall shut their mouths at him: for what had not been told them shall they see, and what they had not heard shall they consider.
x.KJV: So shall he sprinkle many nations; the kings shall shut their mouths at him: for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they consider.
x.YLT: So doth he sprinkle many nations. Concerning him kings shut their mouth, For that which was not recounted to them they have seen, And that which they had not heard they have understood!

nt: Yahweh is speaking of his servant cleansing the people of many nations as if hewould **sprinkle** them the way a priest sprinkled blood or water to purify people and objects. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will cleanse the people of many nations]

The word translated as **sprinkle** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that there is another Hebrew word with the same consonants that in this context would mean “startle.” That may suit the meaning of this verse better. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [he will startle]

Yahweh is using **Kings will shut their mouths** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they will be speechless.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Kings will be silent]
אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹֽא סֻפַּ֤ר לָ⁠הֶם֙ רָא֔וּ וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא שָׁמְע֖וּ הִתְבּוֹנָֽנוּ

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [they will clearly see and understand things about which they had never been told]

The expression **what had not been told to them** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [what no one had told them]
